posts.html:
You do not need a finished brief to start a conversation. You need a clear picture of what is getting in the way.

People often arrive with a solution already picked. “We need Shopify.” “We need a new website.” “We need AI.” Sometimes that is right. Often it is a guess made under pressure. I would rather start with the problem.

If you only have ten minutes, send the URL, what is frustrating, and who currently updates it. That is enough. You can stop there.

If you only have ten minutes

  1. The URL of the site or tool — or a note that there is not one yet.
  2. What is frustrating, outdated, or harder than it should be. One paragraph is plenty.
  3. Who currently updates it, or whether nobody does.

That list is the whole brief. Everything else in this article is optional.

What is actually useful

A first conversation goes better when I can see the system you already have. Not a pitch deck. Not a wishlist of features. The thing people actually use.

The current site or tool. A link is better than a description. If customers look in more than one place — the website, a Google listing, a booking page — send those too. When those disagree, that disagreement is often the project.

What you are trying to get done. Book a table. Find Saturday hours. Apply for a program. Buy something. Call. If visitors cannot do that without phoning you, say so.

Who owns it after the work is done. If one person has the passwords, a former contractor does, or nobody is sure, that belongs in the first message. Ownership is not a later detail. It is the work.

Constraints that are real. A budget range, a season, a grant deadline, a board meeting, staff who are already stretched. I will not use those against you. I need them to recommend something you can actually run.

What you can skip

You do not need to name a platform. You do not need a sitemap. You do not need to collect every login.

Mood boards, plugin lists, and “a site like X” can wait. They are useful later. They are a poor substitute for “customers keep asking the same three questions.”

If you are not sure what the problem is called, that is normal. You do not have to know the technical name. Most projects here start with something that feels outdated, confusing, or harder than it should be.

What happens after you send it

You get a direct reply, not a sales sequence. Typical response time is one to two business days.

We talk about your organization, your customers, and what is actually in the way. I will tell you what I think needs to change, what can wait, and what you can do yourself without spending a cent.

If I am not the right fit, I will say so — and I will still try to point you somewhere useful.

What you can ignore

  • A twenty-page RFP for a first conversation.
  • Rebuilding the site before anyone has looked at it.
  • Hiring anyone to change the hours if you cannot change them yourself.
  • The feeling that you should already know what to ask for.

Start with what is frustrating. We can name it together.

If you have even the ten-minute version, start a conversation. If you want to see how the work is structured first, the About page walks through discovery, recommendations, implementation, and handoff.

posts.html:
A visitor searching from a phone does not think about your website and your Google listing as two systems. They think about Saturday hours, whether you are open, and whether it is worth the drive.

Those answers often live in different places. They drift.

A source of truth is the place where the current hours, rates, or menu actually live — and every other listing is copied from there.

Two sources, one visitor

Your website is the page you (or a developer) update. Your Google Business Profile is a separate listing Google shows in Maps and in search. They do not update each other unless someone makes them.

Add a booking widget, a Facebook page, and a tourism directory, and you can have four versions of the same Saturday in July.

When they disagree, people believe the one they saw first. Then they phone. Or they do not come.

This is not an SEO trick. It is a source-of-truth problem. If you do not have one, you will keep fixing the same mistake in three tools.

Google is how a lot of people find you. The website is the place you control the next step. They do different jobs. They still have to tell the same story about hours, location, and whether someone can book, order, or inquire without calling.

A familiar path

Someone looking up a place in eastern PEI for the weekend sees Google say open until eight. The website, last touched in the off-season, still shows winter hours. The Instagram bio says “see our story for hours.”

None of those people is trying to be difficult. The system has three clocks.

Tourism makes this worse because the facts change: opening day, shoulder season, storm closures, a menu that only exists in July. Staff cannot pause a line to update five platforms. Once the season is underway, the cost of a mismatch is a full inbox and a missed booking.

What to do this week

  1. Pick one place that wins when there is a conflict. For most operators that is either the website or the Google listing — whichever you will actually keep current during the season.
  2. Open the visitor path on a phone: hours, address, and whether they can book, order, or inquire without calling.
  3. Check whether that next step is the same in Google as it is on the site.
  4. Fix the copies that disagree. Do not start a redesign.

If seasonal staff will be the ones changing hours, the winning source has to be something they can edit in ten minutes. If only a developer can change it, it will be wrong by the first holiday.

What you can ignore

  • Paying for a ranking package before the hours match.
  • A new visual theme to “look more professional.”
  • Every directory at once. Start with Google and your own site.

If visitors keep asking questions your site should have answered, the listing and the site are probably telling two stories.

If this is the season problem you are actually in, start on the tourism and hospitality page, or tell me what visitors keep getting wrong.

posts.html:
The request I hear most often is a new website.

Sometimes that is the right work. Often it is the most expensive way to avoid a smaller problem: the site no longer matches the business, customers cannot take the next step, or nobody on the team can change a paragraph without a ticket.

The goal is not more technology. It is a business that works better with the technology it already depends on.

A new theme will not fix that. It can hide it for a season.

What usually needs attention

The information is wrong or hard to find. Services have changed. The booking path sits under three screens of atmosphere. The phone number in the footer is the old one.

The next step is unclear. People who are ready to buy, book, or ask still have to guess. That is not a branding problem.

The tools behind it do not connect. Forms go to an inbox nobody checks. Bookings are retyped into another system. The real hours live in a spreadsheet.

You cannot update it. If changing the hours requires a developer, the site is already more expensive than it looks — and it will be wrong by the first holiday.

I have sat with businesses whose site looked dated and whose actual leak was a form that died on a phone, or a homepage that disagreed with the listing people found first. We repaired those. We did not burn the house down.

When a rebuild is the honest answer

A rebuild is warranted when the structure itself cannot carry the work:

  • Staff cannot edit the pages that have to change.
  • The platform is abandoned, or so patched that every change is a risk.
  • Accessibility is not a missing plugin — the layout cannot work for keyboard or screen readers without starting over.
  • You are asking the site to do a different job (bookings, applications, a store) and the old one was a brochure.

Even then, rebuild the information architecture first. Decide what has to be true, who will update it, and what the next step is. The paint comes last.

A rebuild that leaves you unable to change a photo, a rate, or a typo is not finished. You should leave with the access, documentation, and a system you control — the same standard as a repair.

What you can ignore

  • A competitor’s new site as a reason to panic.
  • Plugin stacks that promise to transform a site you cannot maintain.
  • The idea that looking modern is the same as working.

If something is outdated, confusing, or taking more time than it should, start there. We can decide together whether the honest move is repair, a rebuild, or waiting.

If this sounds like your shop, start with small business services, or tell me what is not working. You do not need to arrive with a solution.
